Take-Home Exercise 2: Be Tradewise or Otherwise

Author

Leng Yi Xiu

Published

March 3, 2025

Modified

March 9, 2025

1 Overview of the Task

Since Mr. Donald Trump took office as the President of the United States on January 20, 2025, one of the most closely watched topics has been global trade.

As a beginner in visual analytics, I will be applying newly learned skills to examine the evolving trends in Singapore’s international trade since 2015 using data and visualisation from Department of Statistics Singapore and Singstat.

The task includes:

  • selecting three data visualisations on this page (Singstat Infographics), comments on the pros and cons and provide sketches of the make-over,

  • creating the make-over of the three data visualisation critic above using appropriate packages, and

  • analysing the data with either time-series analysis or time-series forecasting methods

1.1 Principles of Data Visualisation Design

Before starting on the critic for the 3 data visualisations, we would first need to understand the key principles of data visualisation design.

Firstly, we need to ensure that we are using the right visuals to represent the data and ensure graphical integrity. Snapshots of the data over specific time periods, or across specific groups can be misleading and not representative of any trends.

Visuals should also be simplified, using effective colours and clear labels to provide clarity for the audience. Annotations can be used to provide more insights to the visuals. Lastly, we should aim to create charts that fall within Quadrant 1, where it is clear and aesthetically beautiful.

1.2 The Dataset

The data visualisations on the Singstat Infographics website are on Singapore’s international trade position, mainly describing the trade components and identifying Singapore’s major trading partners from the period of 2020 to 2024. For purpose of the critic and make-over, we will mainly be working with 4 datasets and the datasets have monthly values:

  1. Merchandise Trade By Commodity Section, (At Current Prices)
  2. Merchandise Trade By Region And Selected Market (Imports)
  3. Merchandise Trade By Region And Selected Market (Domestic Exports)
  4. Merchandise Trade By Region And Selected Market (Re-Exports)

1.2.1 Load Packages

pacman::p_load(readxl,tidyverse, tsibble, feasts, fable, 
               seasonal, treemapify, patchwork)

1.3.2 Creating Unique identifiers - Total Merchandise Trade

As the data is structured to have repeated series name (see codes below), we will first need to create unique identifier names to separate between total merchandise, imports, domestic exports and re-exports before summing up the yearly amounts.

Click to view code 
df_mer_trade %>%
  count(`Data Series`, name = "Count") %>%
  filter(Count > 1)
# A tibble: 13 × 2
   `Data Series`                         Count
   <chr>                                 <int>
 1 Animal & Vegetable Oils Fats & Waxes      5
 2 Beverages & Tobacco                       5
 3 Chemicals & Chemical Products             5
 4 Crude Materials (Excl Fuels)              5
 5 Food & Live Animals                       5
 6 Machinery & Transport Equipment           5
 7 Manufactured Goods                        5
 8 Miscellaneous (Excluding Oil Bunkers)     5
 9 Miscellaneous Manufactured Articles       5
10 Non-Oil                                   5
11 Oil                                       5
12 Oil Bunkers                               3
13 Petroleum                                 5
Click to view code 
df_mer_trade <- df_mer_trade %>%
  mutate(ID = case_when(
    between(row_number(), 2, 14) ~ paste0("Tot_", `Data Series`),
    between(row_number(), 16, 27) ~ paste0("Imp_", `Data Series`),
    between(row_number(), 29, 41) ~ paste0("Exp_", `Data Series`),
    between(row_number(), 43, 55) ~ paste0("Dom_", `Data Series`),
    between(row_number(), 57, 68) ~ paste0("ReE_", `Data Series`),
    TRUE ~ paste0(`Data Series`)  # Default values for other rows
  )) %>%
  select(ID, everything())

  )

1.3.4 Merge datasets by region/market into 1 data frame and filter out regions (for Critic #2)

As the datasets for imports and exports by region/market are separated into 3 files, we will have to merge the 3 files together and also filter out the sub-totals to regions in order to have accurate analysis by the trading country:

Click to view code 
yr_grpdf_imports <- grpdf_imports %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`, Year) %>%
  summarize(
    Annual_Amt = sum(Annual_Amt, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

yr_grpdf_dom_exports <- grpdf_dom_exports %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`, Year) %>%
  summarize(
    Annual_Amt = sum(Annual_Amt, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

yr_grpdf_re_exports <- grpdf_re_exports %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`, Year) %>%
  summarize(
    Annual_Amt = sum(Annual_Amt, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

summarized_list <- list(yr_grpdf_dom_exports, yr_grpdf_re_exports, yr_grpdf_imports)
Click to view code 
summarized_tradepartners <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = c("Data Series", "Year"), all = TRUE,
                                                        suffixes = c("_dom_exports", "_re_exports")), summarized_list) %>%
    mutate(`Total Exports` = rowSums(select(., contains("_exports")), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    rename(`Total Imports` = `Annual_Amt`) %>%
    rename(`Countries` = `Data Series`) %>%
    select(`Countries`, `Year`, `Total Exports`, `Total Imports`) %>%
    filter(!`Countries` %in% c("Total All Markets", "America", "Asia", "Europe", "Oceania", "Africa"))

2 Critic & Make-over of Data Visualisations

2.1 Critic #1: Total Merchandise Trade at Current Prices, 2020 - 2024

Data visualisation below aims to show the changes of total merchandise trade at current prices over the period of 5 years:

2.1.1 Pros and Cons of existing data visualisation

✅ Year-on-year increase from previous to current year is clear (Increased 6.6% in 2024)

✅ Chart is sufficiently labelled, with all the amounts standardized to 1 decimal place

❌ Chart only shows year-on-year increase percentage for 1 year, yearly trend is not clear and cannot be visualised as Exports and Imports are separated in 2 bars

❌ Colours used are not visually representative of year, or exports vs imports

❌ Labels showing total amounts by year, but the total amounts cannot be visualised from the chart

2.1.2 Make-over of data visualisation

Click to view code 
summarized_Crit <- grpdf_mer_trade %>%
  filter(ID %in% c("Total Merchandise Imports, (At Current Prices)",
                   "Total Merchandise Exports, (At Current Prices)")) %>%
  group_by(Year, ID) %>%
  summarize(
    Annual_Amt = sum(Annual_Amt, na.rm = TRUE),  
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = ID,  
    values_from = Annual_Amt  
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`Total Merchandise Exports, (At Current Prices)`, 
                        `Total Merchandise Imports, (At Current Prices)`), 
               names_to = "Category", 
               values_to = "Amount") %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Line = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()
Click to view code 
ggplot(summarized_Crit) +
  # Stacked bar chart for Exports and Imports (using the original 'Amount' values for the bars)
  geom_bar(aes(x = as.factor(Year), y = Amount, fill = Category), 
           stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  
  # Add labels to the stacked bars (convert the label values to billions)
  geom_label(aes(x = as.factor(Year), y = Amount, 
                label = paste0(round(Amount / 1e6, 1), " Bil"), fill = Category),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3, color = "black",  label.size = 0) +
  
  # Line for Total Merchandise Trade (sum of Exports and Imports)
  geom_line(aes(x = as.factor(Year), y = Trade_Line, color = "Total Merchandise Trade"), 
            linewidth = 1, group = 1) +
  
  # Add points (markers) on the Trade line (convert the value to billions for display)
  geom_point(aes(x = as.factor(Year), y = Trade_Line, color = "Total Merchandise Trade"), 
             size = 2, shape = 16) +
  
  # Add labels to the points on the Trade line (convert the label values to billions)
  geom_label(aes(x = as.factor(Year), 
                y = Trade_Line, 
                label = paste0(round(Trade_Line / 1e6, 1), " Bil"), 
                color = "black"),
            size = 3, vjust = 0.2, hjust = -0.2, fill = "white",  label.size = 0.1) +
  
  # Labels and theme
  labs(
    title = "Total Merchandise Trade, 2015 - 2024",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Amount (At Current Prices)",
    fill = "Category",
    color = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  
  # Flip axes to make the chart horizontal
  coord_flip() +
  
  # Custom colors for Exports, Imports, and Trade line
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "BuGn") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Total Merchandise Trade" = "darkgrey")) +
  
  # Adjust margins and legend position to avoid clipping
  theme(
    legend.position = "top", 
    legend.justification = "center",
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 20), 
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),  
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),  
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10),  
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.direction = "vertical"
  )
Analysis

We can see clearly from the stacked bar chart above that it can be misleading to show a year-on-year increase in total merchandise trade from 2023 to 2024 as 2023 seems to be an abnormal year after Covid where total merchandise trade decreased by 11.7% from 2022.

2.2 Critic #2: Merchandise Trade Performance with Major Trading Partners, 2024

2.2.1 Pros and Cons of existing data visualisation

✅ Can be visualised clearly which trading partners Singapore’s exports to them exceed our imports from them

✅ Size of bubble reflects the total merchandise trade value well

❌ Bubble plot will not work well if the countries have similar merchandise trade values and the bubbles overlap each other

❌ Not clear on the rankings between trading partners based on total trading volume

Ideal scenario will be like the figure below, where the top 10 trading partners can be clearly visualised with the percentage of exports vs imports clearly seen from the stacked bar chart as well.

2.2.2 Make-over of data visualisation

Click to view code 
# Filter by Year and Rank by Data Series for Top 10
summarized_trade <- summarized_tradepartners %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2024)) %>%  
  mutate(Total_Trade = `Total Exports` + `Total Imports`) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Total_Trade`)) %>%   
  slice_head(n = 10)
Click to view code 
# Convert data to long format for ggplot
summarized_trade <- summarized_trade %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`Total Exports`, `Total Imports`), 
               names_to = "Category", values_to = "Amount") %>%
  mutate(Countries = reorder(Countries, Total_Trade, sum))

# Calculate the percentage for each segment (export/import) relative to the total trade
summarized_trade <- summarized_trade %>%
  mutate(Percentage = Amount / Total_Trade * 100)

  # Stacked bar chart for Exports and Imports 
ggplot(summarized_trade) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = as.factor(Countries), y = Amount, fill = Category), 
           stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
   
  # Add labels to the stacked bars (convert values to billions)
  geom_label(aes(x = as.factor(Countries), y = Amount, 
                label = paste0(round(Percentage, 1), "%"),fill = Category),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3, color = "black", label.size = 0) +
  
  geom_label(data = summarized_trade, 
            aes(x = Countries, y = Total_Trade, 
                label = paste0(round(Total_Trade / 1e3, 1), " Bil")),
            size = 3, color = "black", vjust = 0.2, hjust = -0.2, fill = "white",  label.size = 0.1) +
  
  # Labels and theme
  labs(
    title = "Merchandise Trade Performance with Major Trading Partners, 2024",
    x = "Trading Partners",
    y = "Amount (At Current Prices)",
    fill = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  
  # Flip axes to make the chart horizontal
  coord_flip() +
  
  # Custom colors for Exports and Imports
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "BuGn") +
  
  # Adjust margins and legend position
  theme(
    legend.position = "top", 
    legend.justification = "center",
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 20), 
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),  
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),  
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10),  
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.direction = "horizontal"
  )
Analysis

From the visualisation above, we can see that though countries like China and Malaysia may be Singapore’s largest trading partners, they may not be providing as much trade balances (our exports - imports from them) as a country like Hong Kong or Indonesia.

More insights can be gained if we further look at the major trading partners that we have the highest positive trade balances with.

2.3 Critic #3: Non-Oil Merchandise Trade by Major Commodity Sections, 2024

2.3.1 Pros and Cons of existing data visualisation

✅ Clear indication of the Top 3 commodity sections (separate from the bar chart)

❌ Bar chart does not have consistent colour and fill representation - Machinery & Transport Equipment with dashed fill, but no legend to indicate the difference

❌ Proportion of 87.8% and 83.6% cannot be visualised from the bar chart as it is showing a list of all the different commodity sections

2.3.2 Make-over of data visualisation

Click to view code 
# Summarize exports and get the top 3 exports
top_exports <- grpdf_nonoil %>%
  filter(Category == "Exports", Year == 2024) %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`) %>%
  summarize(Total_Amt = sum(Annual_Amt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(Total_Amt))
  
# Get the top 3 exports by total amount
top_3_exports <- top_exports %>%
  arrange(desc(Total_Amt)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3)

# Add a new category for "Others" to all rows
top_exports <- top_exports %>%
  mutate(Category = ifelse(`Data Series` %in% top_3_exports$`Data Series`, 
                           `Data Series`, "Others"))
tree_data_exp <- top_exports %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarize(Total_Amt = sum(Total_Amt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Calculate percentage for exports
tree_data_exp <- tree_data_exp %>%
  mutate(Percent = Total_Amt / sum(Total_Amt) * 100)

# Summarize imports and get the top 3 imports
top_imports <- grpdf_nonoil %>%
  filter(Category == "Imports", Year == 2024) %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`) %>%
  summarize(Total_Amt = sum(Annual_Amt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(Total_Amt))
  
# Get the top 3 imports by total amount
top_3_imports <- top_imports %>%
  arrange(desc(Total_Amt)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3)

# Add a new category for "Others" to all rows
top_imports <- top_imports %>%
  mutate(Category = ifelse(`Data Series` %in% top_3_imports$`Data Series`, 
                           `Data Series`, "Others"))
tree_data_imp <- top_imports %>%
  group_by(Category) %>%
  summarize(Total_Amt = sum(Total_Amt, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Calculate percentage for imports
tree_data_imp <- tree_data_imp %>%
  mutate(Percent = Total_Amt / sum(Total_Amt) * 100)
Click to view code 
# Create the treemap for exports
export_treemap <- ggplot(tree_data_exp, aes(area = Total_Amt, fill = Category, label = paste0(Category, "\n", round(Percent, 1), "%"))) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_text(color = "black", place = "center", size = 8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel2") +
  labs(title = "Top 3 Exports") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(r = 5))

# Create the treemap for imports with the legend
import_treemap <- ggplot(tree_data_imp, aes(area = Total_Amt, fill = Category, label = paste0(Category, "\n", round(Percent, 1), "%"))) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_text(color = "black", place = "center", size = 8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel2") +
  labs(title = "Top 3 Imports") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")  +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(l = 5))

# Combine the treemaps side by side using patchwork
export_treemap + import_treemap + plot_layout(ncol = 2) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Non-Oil Merchandise Trade by Major Commodity Sections, 2024")

3 Time-Series Analysis

As the datasets used provide details on total exports and imports from various trading partners over the span of 10 years, time-series analysis can be performed.

Using the Top 10 major trading partners of 2024 identified in the previous sections, we can explore a few time-series analysis methods to identify any seasonality and/or trends.

3.1 multiple time-series data with ggplot2 methods

  • Imports
  • Domestic Exports
  • Re-Exports
# Filter by specific countries
countries_top10 <- c("China", "Malaysia", "United States", "Taiwan", "Hong Kong", "Indonesia","Korea, Rep Of", "Japan", "Thailand","India")

ggplot(data = grpdf_imports %>%
         filter(`Data Series` %in% countries_top10), 
       aes(x = `Year_Month_Date`, 
           y = Annual_Amt,
           color = `Data Series`)) +
  geom_line(size = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Month-Year",
    y = "Amount (Mil)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom", 
    legend.box.spacing = unit(0.5, "cm")
  )

Analysis

Imports:

  • China has historically over the last 10 years been a trading partner that Singapore has gotten the most imports from.

  • However in recent years, there is a spike in our imports from neighbouring countries, especially Malaysia.

  • Overall imports have been on an increasing trend from 2015 to 2024, suggesting that Singapore is becoming more reliant on imports, particular from 4 countries - Taiwan, Malaysia, China and US.

Domestic Exports:

  • Again, Singapore has been consistently exporting to China over the last 10 years.

  • Domestic exports to US is seasonal and spikes around once a year.

Re-Exports:

  • Singapore re-exports mainly to Hong Kong and China.
